front: {{c1::Pacinian}} corpuscles sense deep pressure/vibration; {{c2::Meissner}} corpuscles light touch; Merkel discs texture; Ruffini endings stretch.
why: Mechanoreceptor roster is prep-book somatosensation; AAMC outline only names pain explicitly

front: {{c1::Presbyopia}} is age-related loss of lens accommodation for near vision; {{c2::presbycusis}} is age-related high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss.
why: Age-related presbyopia/presbycusis is clinical vocabulary beyond the 6A outline

front: {{c1::Size constancy}} holds perceived size steady as distance changes the retinal image; {{c2::shape constancy}} holds perceived shape steady as slant changes.
why: Perceptual constancies are named on the 6A outline and asked directly

front: A patient with V1 destruction denies seeing anything yet reliably points to lights in the blind field. Name this and its anatomical explanation.
why: Blindsight is neuroscience trivia; a passage would define it if used

front: A person consistently experiences the numeral 7 as green. Name the phenomenon and the leading neural account.
why: Synesthesia and its cross-activation account are trivia-grade for the MCAT

front: A radiologist told 'never miss a tumor' shifts to a liberal criterion. What happens to hits and false alarms?
why: Criterion shift reasoning (hits and false alarms both rise) is the classic SDT question

front: A retinal ganglion cell with an {{c1::on-center, off-surround}} receptive field is nearly silent under diffuse light because of {{c2::lateral inhibition}}.
why: Center-surround fields support lateral inhibition; the Mach-band card is the plainer version

front: A subject notices 2 g added to a 100 g weight. Per Weber's law, how much must be added to 500 g to be noticed?
why: Weber's law calculation is the formula item for this topic

front: After staring at a green square, a viewer sees a red patch on white paper. Which theory of color vision does this support, and by what mechanism?
why: Afterimages via opponent-process is the standard color-vision question

front: An amputee feels burning in a missing hand and reports hand sensations when his cheek is touched. What explains both findings?
why: Phantom limb cortical remapping is neuroplasticity trivia outside 6A core

front: At the optic chiasm, fibers from the {{c1::nasal}} halves of each retina cross, so each hemisphere processes the {{c2::contralateral}} visual field.
why: Optic chiasm nasal crossing and contralateral fields are a frequently tested pathway fact

front: Cochlear hair cells depolarize when tip links pull open channels admitting {{c1::potassium (K+)}}, which is unusually concentrated in the {{c2::endolymph}}.
why: K+-rich endolymph transduction detail is physiology beyond the AAMC psych outline

front: Conductive hearing loss results from:
why: Conductive vs sensorineural loss is a common second-step distinction in hearing items

front: Contrast bottom-up and top-down processing.
why: Bottom-up vs top-down processing is named on the outline and asked directly

front: Describe the time course of dark adaptation and the 'rod-cone break'.
why: Dark-adaptation minute values and rod-cone break are numeric trivia not on the outline

front: Distinguish proprioception, kinesthesia, and the vestibular sense, and name the receptors for each.
why: Kinesthetic and vestibular senses are outline items; receptor roster is supporting detail

front: Distinguish sensation from perception.
why: Sensation vs perception is a definition needed for understanding, rarely a point itself

front: Distinguish sensory adaptation from habituation, including where each occurs.
why: Sensory adaptation vs habituation is a high-frequency distinction

front: Fechner's law: sensation grows {{c1::logarithmically}} with stimulus intensity; Stevens' law instead uses a {{c2::power}} function.
why: Fechner log vs Stevens power law is second-tier psychophysics

front: Gestalt: {{c1::closure}} makes us perceive incomplete figures as whole, and {{c2::pragnanz}} says perception defaults to the simplest stable organization.
why: Closure and pragnanz are secondary Gestalt principles; the roster card is primary

front: Give two unusual properties of olfactory receptor neurons compared with most neurons.
why: Olfactory neuron regeneration and one-receptor-per-neuron are trivia beyond the outline

front: How does the volley principle rescue frequency theory above ~1000 Hz?
why: Volley principle is a second step behind place vs frequency theory

front: How is the absolute threshold operationally defined in psychophysics?
why: Absolute threshold as 50% detection is core threshold content

front: In {{c1::myopia}} the image focuses in front of the retina and needs a diverging lens; in {{c2::hyperopia}} it focuses behind and needs a converging lens.
why: Myopia/hyperopia lens correction is askable but mostly tested via C/P optics

front: In Rubin's vase, the image flips between a vase and two faces. Which gestalt principle is at work, and why does the flip occur?
why: Figure-ground via Rubin's vase is a standard Gestalt illustration

front: In signal detection terms, screening {{c1::sensitivity}} is the hit rate and {{c2::specificity}} is the correct-rejection rate.
why: Mapping sensitivity/specificity onto SDT is a useful cross-section second step

front: In signal detection theory, {{c1::d-prime (d')}} indexes sensitivity, while the {{c2::criterion}} reflects response bias — the strategy for saying yes.
why: d-prime vs criterion is the core signal-detection distinction

front: Motion parallax: as you move, near objects appear to sweep {{c1::opposite}} to your motion while distant objects seem to move {{c2::with}} you.
why: Motion parallax is a named monocular cue; secondary to the cue-family card

front: Name the main Gestalt principles.
why: Gestalt principle roster is asked directly

front: Name the two binocular depth cues and state which one dominates at very close range.
why: Retinal disparity vs convergence is supporting detail on the binocular cue card

front: Olfaction is the only sense that bypasses the {{c1::thalamus}}, projecting from the olfactory bulb directly to {{c2::limbic}} structures.
why: Olfaction bypassing the thalamus is a classic discrete item

front: Opponent-process theory explains:
why: Restates the afterimage/opponent-process card (8), which carries the mechanism

front: People from non-carpentered, rural societies are less fooled by the Muller-Lyer illusion. What does this cross-cultural result imply about perception?
why: Muller-Lyer cross-cultural result illustrates top-down/cultural influence in passages

front: Per Melzack and Wall's gate control theory, why does rubbing an injury reduce pain?
why: Gate control theory is the named pain-perception mechanism on the outline

front: Place theory best explains perception of:
why: Place vs frequency theory of pitch is asked directly

front: Radiologists told a chest film came from a smoker report more nodules than those given no history. Name the effect and the processing it illustrates.
why: Radiology expectancy scenario illustrates perceptual set; plain definition card exists

front: Railroad tracks seem to meet in the distance. Which monocular cue is this, and how does interposition differ?
why: Linear perspective vs interposition are named monocular cues; secondary to the family card

front: Red-green color deficiency is {{c1::X-linked recessive}} and far more common in {{c2::males}}; blue-yellow (tritan) defects are rare and not sex-linked.
why: X-linked inheritance of color blindness is genetics content, not 6A perception

front: Signal detection: on a noise-only trial the subject reports a signal. What outcome is this?
why: The SDT 2x2 outcome matrix is asked directly

front: Signal detection: the signal is present but the subject says no. Name the outcome and the criterion shift that makes it more common.
why: Miss plus conservative-criterion shift is the mirror of the liberal-criterion card

front: Sound localization relies primarily on:
why: Interaural time/intensity cues are askable auditory localization content

front: State Weber's law.
why: Weber's law statement is core psychophysics

front: Subliminal primes reliably shift a nearby rating slightly but do not make people buy things they do not want. What does this show about thresholds?
why: Subliminal processing below threshold is an outline point; passage-flavored here

front: Sweet, umami, and bitter tastes are transduced by {{c1::G protein-coupled receptors}}; salty and sour by {{c2::ion channels}}.
why: Taste transduction split (GPCR vs channel) is supporting detail on gustation

front: The {{c1::magnocellular}} pathway carries motion and depth with high temporal resolution; the {{c2::parvocellular}} pathway carries color and fine detail.
why: Magno/parvo pathways support the parallel-processing item; prep-book depth

front: The {{c1::parasympathetic}} nervous system constricts pupils; the {{c2::sympathetic}} system dilates them.
why: Autonomic pupil control is simple and askable, though it sits closer to nervous-system content

front: The {{c1::ventral}} 'what' stream runs to the temporal lobe for object identity; the {{c2::dorsal}} 'where and how' stream runs to the parietal lobe.
why: Ventral/dorsal streams appear in passages; secondary to core visual pathway

front: The rod pigment {{c1::rhodopsin}} is the protein opsin bound to {{c2::retinal}}, a vitamin A derivative that changes shape when it absorbs light.
why: Rhodopsin/retinal and vitamin A night blindness is supporting phototransduction detail

front: Tonotopy: the {{c1::base}} of the cochlea (narrow, stiff) transduces high frequencies, while the {{c2::apex}} (wide, floppy) transduces low frequencies.
why: Tonotopy base/apex is supporting detail on place theory

front: Trace the main visual pathway from optic chiasm to cortex, naming the thalamic relay.
why: Retina to LGN to V1 pathway is a core visual processing item

front: Vestibular sense: contrast what the semicircular canals detect versus the otolith organs.
why: Canals vs otoliths is the askable vestibular distinction

front: Weber's law: the just noticeable difference is a {{c1::constant proportion}} of the original stimulus intensity, called the {{c2::Weber fraction}}.
why: Restates the plain Weber's law card (41)

front: What are monocular vs. binocular depth cues?
why: Monocular vs binocular depth cues are asked directly

front: What did Hubel and Wiesel discover by recording from cat visual cortex?
why: Feature detectors are on the outline; Hubel and Wiesel history is secondary

front: What does signal detection theory add to threshold models?
why: Conceptual framing of SDT; the d-prime/criterion card carries the point

front: What happens electrically to a rod photoreceptor when light strikes it?
why: Rod hyperpolarization in light is a classic trick fact; supporting phototransduction

front: What is parallel processing in vision, and why does it make perception fast?
why: Parallel processing is named on the outline; conceptual card

front: What is sensory adaptation?
why: Plain sensory adaptation definition; the adaptation vs habituation card is primary

front: Which cells transmit visual signals from the retina to the brain?
why: Retinal cell order and ganglion cells forming the optic nerve is asked directly

front: Which lobes process vision, hearing, and touch?
why: Lobe-to-sense mapping is basic and askable

front: Which of the following best describes perceptual set?
why: Perceptual set definition supports top-down processing items

front: Which receptors serve kinesthesia, and what does each monitor?
why: Restates the proprioception/kinesthesia receptor card (15)

front: Which two interaural cues localize sound, and which brainstem structure first compares them?
why: Restates the sound-localization card (40); superior olive is trivia

front: Why are rods more sensitive in dim light but poorer at acuity than cones?
why: Rod vs cone sensitivity/acuity via convergence is a core vision item

front: Why do the borders between adjacent gray bands look exaggerated, and which retinal cells produce this?
why: Lateral inhibition and Mach bands are a common passage mechanism

front: Why does stubbing a toe produce sharp then dull pain? Name the fiber types.
why: A-delta vs C fiber pain is supporting somatosensation detail

front: Why does the fovea have the highest visual acuity?
why: Fovea acuity restates the rod/cone convergence idea with the fovea as example

front: Why is the two-point threshold tiny on fingertips but huge on the back?
why: Two-point threshold and receptor density is passage-plausible reasoning

front: You group an array of dots into columns because dots in each column share a color. Which gestalt principle — and which one would grouping by nearness be?
why: Similarity vs proximity is a worked example of the Gestalt roster
